newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Belgian Telinfo sees bright future.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Belgian Telinfo sees bright future.

text.p: Belgian data communications firm Telinfo said on Friday it expected a rise in 1997 group pre-tax profit of 20 percent due to mushrooming use of GSM mobile phones, the Internet and digitalisation.

"I foresee growth of about 20 percent -- group pre-tax profit -- and of 17 percent in turnover in 1997," chairman John Cordier told a news conference on 1996 earnings. In 1996 group net profit soared 74 percent to 221 million francs.
Cordier signed several lucrative contracts around the New Year, which would help Telinfo reach its goals.
"Just before or after New Year we were awarded a number of important agreements...and January looks like it is going to be a top month, it exceeded all expectations."
He said Telecom Italia awarded it a contract worth 130 million Belgian francs ($3.86 million) to supply switching gear.
Telinfo also obtained a contract worth 80 to 85 million francs from a Polish telecoms company for high-speed modems which allow analogue lines to be digitalised.
The digitalisation of analogue equipment would be one of the backbones of future growth for the company.

"This is a new product which we brought on to the market at the end of 1996...There is a lot of interest for the product which we developed ourselves," Cordier said. In Belgium alone there were 80,000 analogue circuits which had to be digitalised.
Telinfo recently won a deal with leading Belgian bank Generale Bank worth 80 million francs.

In addition, it won a contract late last year from Belgian telecommunications start-up Telenet Operaties NV, which aims to convert Flanders' extensive cable television network to provide multimedia and voice telephone services from late 1997.
Telindus Nortel, a joint venture between Telinfo and Canada's Northern Telecom, will supply Telenet's digital telephone exchanges.
An expected surge in use of GSM mobile phones and the Internet and Intranets in the years ahead would bolster Telinfo's business, he said.

Telinfo -- 41 percent-owned by a consortium comprising Belgian steel maker Sidmar NV, a unit of Luxembourg's Arbed and Belgium's Cordier Group -- said it achieved its goals for 1996 despite hefty investments.

It injected 1.1 billion francs for a 10 percent stake in Belgian-French company Mobistar, which operates Belgium's second GSM mobile phone network. France Telecom has 62 percent and a group of eight other Belgian investors 28 percent.
Telinfo said Mobistar would raise capital by two billion francs in 1997 to develop its network. Telinfo will finance its share of the capital boost with its own cash flow.
Mobistar has signed up 68,000 subscribers four months after its launch, 42,000 more than expected.
Cordier declined to give details on acquisition plans but said Telinfo was trying to see how it could become number one -- in corporate data communications -- in other countries.

"Data communications is still unexplored territory," he said. He said Telinfo had a market share of about 65 percent in Belgium and between 75 and 80 percent in Luxembourg where the state, European Union and major banks were among its clients.
Telinfo would continue to invest in Asia but that it would take time to reap benefits. Telinfo's share of turnover from outside Europe stayed at two percent in 1996.
Group turnover rose primarily in Germany, Italy and Britain in 1996. The share of the Benelux countries in turnover fell to 79 percent from 84 percent a year earlier.
